about: The priest spreads his hands over the offerings — a gesture the Roman Mass uses in this one place only — and the server rings the bell: the sign that the consecration is near. The second half of the prayer, from diésque nostros, was added by St Gregory the Great, according to the Liber Pontificalis. The petition hangs on quǽsumus: the ut-clause — that Thou accept — is carried by this one we beseech.

s01.narrative: The priest holds his hands spread over the offerings.

s02.translation: Therefore, Lord, we pray: graciously accept this oblation of our service, that of Your whole family;

s03.translation: order our days in Your peace, and command that we be delivered from eternal damnation and counted among the flock of those You have chosen.

w001.function: It points at what the priest is at this moment holding his hands over.

w004.function: A genitive: the offering “of our service” — of those who stand at the altar; the wider pair, “famíliæ” (w009), follows at once.

w009.function: A genitive paired with “servitútis” (w004): after the service of the altar, the whole household of God — the Church.

w011.function: Often a fossilised parenthesis; here it governs: the clause with “ut” (w013) hangs on this verb of asking.

w014.function: The adjective agrees with the unstated subject of “accípias” (w015): not be appeased, but receive already appeased.

w016.function: Accusative plural; the -que attached to it joins this clause to the one before.

w026.function: The accusative subject of the infinitive “éripi” (w027): bid that we be snatched away.

w027.function: A passive infinitive depending on “iúbeas” (w032), five words further on; the same verb governs “numerári” (w034) as well.

w033.function: An ablative under “in” (w029): numbered within the flock, not added to it.

w036.function: No eúndem here: Christ has not been named in this prayer, so there is nothing to refer back to.
